idiom_name: Enumerable.Where with Func<T, bool> / Predicate<T> (deferred execution)
implementation_notes: The criterion is a delegate: Enumerable.Where<TSource>(IEnumerable<TSource>, Func<TSource, bool>), with Predicate<T> available for List<T>.FindAll/RemoveAll and the Contains/Exists family. A container-typed filtered copy is a two-line method - public System Filtered(Func<Threat, bool> keep) => new(SystemId, Threats.Where(keep).ToImmutableArray()); - and because Where is documented as deferred execution the query itself is a first-class criterion holder that can be stored and re-enumerated before it is materialised. Predicate<T> carries no logical combinators (unlike java.util.function.Predicate), so named criteria are extension methods, static Func fields or boolean expressions inside one lambda. Use this form for in-memory data; use the expression-tree variant when the criterion must be translated by a query provider.
pitfalls: Deferred execution: Where returns a query, not a result - enumerating it twice re-runs the predicate and sees any mutation made in between, so materialise (ToArray/ToImmutableArray) before handing out a container-typed copy.
On an IQueryable source the Enumerable.Where overload (Func<T, bool>) still compiles, which pulls the whole table into memory for client-side filtering - the classic accidental full-table scan.
Criteria stored on long-lived objects capture their closures: a filter that refers to a large object graph keeps it alive, and mutable captured state makes the criterion order-dependent.

variants.name: Queryable provider with an expression-tree criterion
variants.idiom_name: IQueryable<T>.Where(Expression<Func<T, bool>>) translated by the provider
variants.implementation_notes: When the elements live in a store, the criterion stays first-class but as an expression tree: IQueryable<Threat>.Where(Expression<Func<Threat, bool>>) lets the provider (EF Core, LINQ to SQL) inspect the predicate and translate it, usually to SQL, so the filter runs where the data is and the filtered result is whatever the provider materialises. This is a different mechanism with different limits: only expression-shaped code is translatable, closures must be lifted into parameters, and an untranslatable criterion fails at run time rather than compile time - so keep criteria on the provider's supported subset and test the translation, or split the work (server-side pre-filter plus an in-memory Where).
pitfalls: Untranslatable predicates throw at run time (or silently fall back to client evaluation on older providers): keep to the provider's supported expression subset and cover the translation with a test.
Expression trees cannot contain statement bodies, out/ref, dynamic or arbitrary helper calls, so a criterion that reads naturally in memory must be rewritten to be translatable.
Captured variables become query parameters - usually what you want - but captured objects the provider cannot parameterise either fail or are evaluated client-side; hoist values into locals first.
